title: The Thirteenth Century
orientation: This chapter surveys the political and religious events that formed the mental atmosphere of the thirteenth century -- the culmination of the medieval synthesis -- centering on the towering figures of Pope Innocent III and Emperor Frederick II, the great medieval heresies (Cathari/Albigenses, Waldenses), the founding of the Inquisition, and the mendicant orders of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic. It matters because it sets the political and institutional stage (papal supremacy, the friars' rise to intellectual leadership) on which the scholastic philosophy of Aquinas, treated in the next chapter, was built.
historical_background: Russell presents the thirteenth century as the point at which the medieval synthesis -- built up gradually since the fall of Rome -- reached its most complete form, embodied in towering figures (Innocent III, Saint Francis, Frederick II, Aquinas) and achievements (Gothic cathedrals, Magna Carta, the beginnings of the House of Commons). Innocent III (1198-1216) pushed papal claims to their historical maximum, securing acknowledgments of papal overlordship from England, Portugal, Aragon, and effectively directing the Fourth Crusade (diverted to Constantinople) and the brutal Albigensian Crusade. His ward Frederick II, culturally cosmopolitan but politically reactionary, fought a decades-long, ultimately losing war against the papacy and the Lombard cities, while heretical movements (Cathari, Waldenses) exposed deep popular discontent with clerical wealth and corruption that the Church met with the new mendicant orders and, from 1233, the Inquisition.
philosophical_problems: How the professed archaism/orthodoxy of an institution (the Church) can coexist with, and even enable, its use of naked political power (Innocent III as 'the first great Pope in whom there was no element of sanctity')

Why heretical popular movements (Cathari, Waldenses) arose despite lacking support from secular rulers, and what this reveals about the relationship between religious dissent and political power in the period

The tension, illustrated by the fate of the Franciscan order, between an ideal of radical poverty/simplicity and the institutional pressures (wealth, power, doctrinal orthodoxy) that tend to corrupt religious movements
Whether reason independent of dogma can flourish under institutions (like Frederick II's court) that combine genuine intellectual openness with politically retrograde absolutism
schools_discussed: The Cathari (Albigenses), a dualist heresy descended from the Bogomiles, Paulicians, and ultimately Manichaeanism
The Waldenses, followers of Peter Waldo, who rejected clerical mediation and appointed their own ministers
The Franciscan order (mendicant, emphasizing radical poverty)
The Dominican order (mendicant, emphasizing learning and combating heresy)

core_concepts.name: The papal-imperial power struggle under Innocent III and Frederick II
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Innocent III pushed the medieval papacy's claims to temporal supremacy further than any pope before him, securing formal submission from England, Portugal, and Aragon, and installing his own ward, the young Frederick II, as Emperor. But Frederick grew into a formidable, culturally brilliant but politically reactionary ruler whose decades-long conflict with successive popes -- fueled by his refusal to crusade promptly, his negotiated (rather than military) recovery of Jerusalem, and his ambitions in Italy -- ended in stalemate at his death, with the papacy narrowly triumphant but at lasting cost to its moral authority.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The extended thirteenth-century conflict between the papacy (Innocent III and his successors) and the Holy Roman Empire (chiefly Frederick II), fought over control of Italy, the Sicilian kingdom, Crusading obligations, and ultimate sovereignty between spiritual and temporal power.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It represents the political culmination of the conflict traced through the preceding two chapters, and its outcome -- papal victory over the Empire, but at the cost of moral prestige -- sets up the decline of papal authority treated in Chapter XV.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Begins with Innocent III's accession in 1198 and Frederick II's minority under his guardianship; intensifies after Frederick's own accession as Emperor in 1212 and continues until Frederick's death in 1250.
examples: Frederick's negotiated recovery of Jerusalem from the Muslims in 1229 while still under excommunication, angering the Pope more than his earlier refusal to crusade at all
Frederick's new legal code for Sicily, minting of 'augustals' (the first Western gold coinage in centuries), and founding of the University of Naples
Frederick's mutilation and persecution of plotters, and the suicide of his former minister Pietro della Vigna after being blinded on suspicion of treachery
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The political vacuum and mutual exhaustion left by Frederick's death contributed to the fragmentation of Italy and the eventual thirteenth-to-fourteenth-century decline of both imperial and (more gradually) papal power, treated further in Chapter XV.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Illustrates the thoroughly entangled character of thirteenth-century politics and religion: crusading obligation, heresy, and territorial ambition were all simultaneously religious and political instruments.

core_concepts.name: The Cathari (Albigensian) heresy and its persecution
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The Cathari, strongest in southern France (where they were called Albigenses), were dualists who believed matter itself was evil, created by a wicked demiurge (identified with the Old Testament God), and that only the New Testament revealed the true, good God. They rejected the resurrection of the body, practiced strict asceticism (vegetarianism excepting fish, rejection of marriage) for an elite class of 'the perfected,' while ordinary adherents lived more normal lives. Innocent III called a Crusade against them in 1209, conducted with great ferocity, and the movement was ultimately stamped out through war and, from 1233, the newly founded Inquisition.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A dualist heretical movement, descended via the Bogomiles of Bulgaria from the Paulicians and ultimately Manichaeanism, holding that matter is evil and that the created world is the work of a wicked demiurge distinct from the true, good God revealed in the New Testament.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Its scale and popularity (including among southern French nobility) exposed how widely the wealth and moral corruption of the clergy had alienated ordinary believers, motivating the Church's crackdown via Crusade and the institutional invention of the Inquisition.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell from Marcion (ca. 150 AD) and the Gnostics, through the Paulicians (an Armenian sect) and the Bogomiles of Bulgaria, reaching Italy and southern France via contact during the Crusades; a Bulgarian delegation attended a Cathari council near Toulouse in 1167.
examples: Cathari vegetarianism, with an exception for fish (believed not to be sexually generated)
The Cathari view that marriage is worse than adultery because it is 'continuous and complacent'
The distinction between the ordinary faithful and the 'perfected,' who alone were held to strict precepts
objections: Russell cautions that Cathari doctrine is known 'with certainty' only through hostile testimony, and that persecutors, being versed in the history of heresy, tended to attribute the tenets of older sects to new ones on the basis of loose resemblance
competing_positions: Orthodox Catholic doctrine, which affirmed the goodness of the created material world and the resurrection of the body
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The Albigensian Crusade (1209) and the 1233 founding of the Inquisition by Gregory IX to combat this and related heresies established institutional and legal machinery (denial of counsel after 1254, confiscation of property, handover to the 'secular arm') that persisted for centuries and was later used, for instance, against Joan of Arc.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Many southern French nobles supported the Cathari partly for the opportunity to seize Church lands, illustrating how religious dissent and material/political interest were intertwined.

core_concepts.name: Saint Francis, the Franciscan order, and its ironic institutional fate
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Saint Francis of Assisi renounced wealth after a sudden act of compassion toward a leper, founding an order of followers vowed to complete, radical poverty (begging their bread, refusing even houses or churches). Innocent III shrewdly recognized the order in 1209/1210, keeping it within orthodoxy rather than letting it become another heretical 'Poor Men of Lyons.' But within a generation of Francis's death, his own order abandoned poverty (his successor Brother Elias 'wallowed in luxury'), became a recruiting arm for factional wars, staffed much of the Inquisition, and condemned as heretical (in 1323) the 'Spirituals' who tried to remain faithful to Francis's original ideal.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The mendicant religious order founded by Saint Francis of Assisi (recognized by Innocent III, 1209/1210), originally committed to absolute poverty and itinerant preaching, whose subsequent institutional history (wealth, involvement in the Inquisition, persecution of its own 'Spiritual' faction) Russell presents as a bitterly ironic betrayal of its founder's aims.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It illustrates, for Russell, a recurring historical pattern in which a genuinely selfless religious impulse is captured and redirected by institutional and political interests -- and it sets up the later chapter on Franciscan schoolmen (Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, Occam), the order that, ironically, produced the most independent-minded philosophers of the following century.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Founded by Saint Francis of Assisi (1181/1182-1226) following his renunciation of his family's wealth; formally recognized by Innocent III in 1209 or 1210.
examples: Francis's hymn to the sun, written shortly before his death, which Russell compares to the sun-worship of Akhnaton while noting it remains distinctly Christian
Francis's 1219 journey to preach before the Muslim sultan, who received him courteously but did not convert
Francis's distress on returning to find his followers had built themselves a permanent house, contrary to his ideal of total poverty
competing_positions: Saint Dominic's order, which prioritized learning and doctrinal combat over Francis's radical poverty ideal from the start
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The later Franciscan intellectual tradition (Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, William of Occam), despite Francis's own personal dislike of learning, becomes the source of the most philosophically original scholastics of the following century, as the next chapter notes.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Franciscans became chief conductors of the Inquisition in several countries and recruiting agents in the wars of Guelfs and Ghibellines -- outcomes Russell judges to be the 'most bitterly ironical' possible given Francis's own character and aims.

key_distinctions: Cathari 'perfected' (bound by strict ascetic precepts) vs. ordinary believers (permitted to eat meat and marry)
The Franciscans' original ideal of absolute poverty vs. the order's actual institutional wealth and power after Francis's death
The Church's professed spiritual mission vs. its concrete pursuit of temporal power, most starkly embodied in Innocent III

Secular rulers' general refusal to ally with heretics vs. popular/noble sympathy for heretical movements like the Cathari, explained by the absence of any existing philosophy reconciling heresy with royal claims to dominion
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The Cathari's dualism and rejection of the material world as evil directly continues a lineage Russell traces back through the Bogomiles and Paulicians to Marcion and the Gnostics of the second century AD, connecting this chapter's heresies to strands of thought discussed in earlier volumes on the ancient world.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The Dominican order's institutional commitment to reconciling Aristotle and Christian doctrine (via Albertus Magnus and, above all, Thomas Aquinas) is introduced here as the direct set-up for the following chapter; the eventual philosophical prominence of Franciscans (Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, William of Occam) despite Francis's own anti-intellectualism is explicitly flagged as the subject of chapters to come.
political_social_context: Innocent III's pontificate marks the high-water mark of papal claims to temporal supremacy (formal submissions from King John of England, Portugal, and Aragon); the long Guelf-Ghibelline conflict between pro-papal and pro-imperial factions, and the diversion of the Fourth Crusade to the commercial advantage of Venice rather than to Jerusalem, both show how thoroughly religious institutions and rhetoric were harnessed to concrete political and commercial interests throughout the century.
religion_science_culture_context: The wide popular appeal of heresies like the Cathari and Waldenses is attributed by Russell mainly to 'moral disgust at the wealth and wickedness of the clergy' rather than doctrinal persuasion -- a discontent Russell explicitly likens to the forces that 'ultimately led to the Reformation,' though thirteenth-century secular rulers, unlike sixteenth-century ones, were not yet willing to side with heretics against Rome.
russell_presentation: Russell portrays Innocent III bluntly as 'the first great Pope in whom there was no element of sanctity,' a shrewd and highly successful power-politician whose reforms of Church administration entrenched a hierarchy 'convinced that it need no longer trouble to be holy.' He treats Frederick II with evident personal admiration for his cosmopolitan learning and cultural openness ('one of the most remarkable rulers known to history'), while judging his politics 'retrograde' and his ultimate failure inevitable, since his aims (restoring something like the pagan Roman Empire) put him at odds with the genuinely popular and quasi-democratic forces of his day. Russell is openly moved by the story of Saint Francis, calling him 'one of the most lovable men known to history,' and treats the corruption of the Franciscan order after Francis's death as an almost tragic irony -- 'if Satan existed, the future of the order... would afford him the most exquisite gratification.' Throughout, Russell's tone toward the Church's institutional exercise of power (Crusades, Inquisition, persecution of Jews and heretics) is critical and unsparing, even while he credits genuine intellectual and cultural achievements of the century.
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism: modern historians of the Cathari (e.g. in the wake of research since the mid-twentieth century) have questioned how far the movement really constituted a single coherent 'Manichaean' theology transmitted intact from the Bogomiles, suggesting Inquisitorial sources (which Russell relies on, while flagging their bias) may have systematized and exaggerated doctrinal coherence that was in practice more localized and varied.
key_takeaways: Innocent III (1198-1216) brought papal claims to temporal supremacy to their historical peak, securing formal submissions from England, Portugal, and Aragon.
Frederick II, Innocent's own ward, became a culturally brilliant but politically reactionary Emperor whose decades-long conflict with the papacy ended in stalemate at his death in 1250.

The Cathari (Albigenses), a dualist heresy tracing back through the Bogomiles and Paulicians to Marcion and the Gnostics, was suppressed by the Albigensian Crusade (from 1209) and the newly founded Inquisition (1233).

Saint Francis founded the Franciscan order on an ideal of radical poverty, but within a generation the order abandoned that ideal, staffed the Inquisition, and persecuted its own 'Spiritual' faithful.
Saint Dominic's order, by contrast, was devoted to learning and doctrinal combat from the start, producing Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas.

Russell attributes the thirteenth century's popular heresies mainly to moral revulsion at clerical wealth and corruption, comparing the underlying motives to those that later produced the Reformation.
study_notes:
This chapter is primarily narrative history rather than philosophy, and its purpose is to establish the political, institutional, and religious backdrop against which Aquinas's philosophy (next chapter) and the Franciscan schoolmen (two chapters later) must be understood. Pay particular attention to two institutional facts that recur later: first, that the Dominican order's early and deliberate commitment to scholarship (in contrast to Dominic's own personal anti-intellectualism) is what produced Albertus Magnus and Aquinas; second, that the Franciscan order, despite Francis's own dislike of learning, later produced Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, and William of Occam -- meaning the order most associated with anti-establishment poverty became, ironically, the intellectual home of scholasticism's most independent late voices.

Also notice how Russell uses Frederick II as a case study in the limits of individual enlightenment against structural political position: however personally tolerant and cosmopolitan Frederick was (friendly with Muslims, fluent in six languages, founder of a university), his position as Emperor structurally required him to oppose the politically liberal, quasi-democratic forces (free cities, even some heretics) that might otherwise have been natural allies against the papacy. This is a useful example of Russell's general method of reading individual character against structural political constraint.

Finally, the founding of the Inquisition (1233) deserves attention as an institutional innovation with a long afterlife: originally created to handle the practical burden of heresy prosecution that had outgrown ordinary episcopal capacity, its procedures (denial of counsel after 1254, property confiscation, handover to secular authorities for execution) became a durable model of religious persecution used well beyond its original Albigensian target, as Russell notes with the example of Joan of Arc.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A dualist religious movement, strongest in southern France, that believed the material world was created by an evil power and that true goodness belonged only to a separate spiritual God.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A medieval dualist heresy, descended via the Bogomiles and Paulicians from Manichaean and Gnostic sources, holding matter to be inherently evil and rejecting the Old Testament creator-God in favor of a distinct, purely spiritual good God revealed in the New Testament; suppressed by the Albigensian Crusade (from 1209) and the Inquisition.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Followers of Peter Waldo who gave up their possessions, preached poverty, and eventually rejected the authority of Catholic priests.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A reformist religious movement founded by Peter Waldo around 1170, initially papally approved but condemned in 1184 after criticizing clerical immorality; they appointed their own ministers independent of the Catholic priesthood and spread to Lombardy and Bohemia, where they influenced the later Hussites.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Church institution founded to investigate and prosecute heresy, using harsh methods including torture and execution.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A judicial institution founded by Gregory IX in 1233, primarily staffed by Dominicans and Franciscans, to systematize the prosecution of heresy (and later sorcery and witchcraft) previously handled less formally by bishops; denied the accused counsel after 1254 and handed convicted heretics to secular authorities for execution.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The names of the two rival factions in medieval Italian politics: Guelfs supported the Pope, Ghibellines supported the Emperor.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Corruptions of 'Welf' and 'Waiblingen,' the family names of rival claimants to the imperial throne at the time of Frederick's contest with Emperor Otto; the terms subsequently named the pro-papal (Guelf) and pro-imperial (Ghibelline) factions across Italian city politics.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Religious orders, like the Franciscans and Dominicans, whose members took vows of poverty and lived by begging rather than owning property.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Thirteenth-century religious orders (chiefly Franciscan and Dominican) founded on a rule of corporate and individual poverty, sustained by alms rather than fixed endowments; they came to dominate both popular preaching and, in the Dominican case especially, university scholarship.
related_concepts: Saint Francis, the Franciscan order, and its ironic institutional fate

questions.prompt: In what ways did Pope Innocent III bring papal claims to temporal power to their peak, and what does Russell mean by calling him a Pope 'in whom there was no element of sanctity'?
questions.answer: Innocent secured formal acknowledgments of papal overlordship from England (King John), Portugal, and Aragon; guided (if reluctantly) the Fourth Crusade's diversion to Constantinople; and called the Albigensian Crusade. Russell means that Innocent was a shrewd, highly effective political operator who advanced Church power through statecraft rather than personal holiness, reflecting a broader shift in which the reformed Church, having secured its moral prestige, 'need no longer trouble to be holy.'
questions.explanation: This judgment sets up the pattern of moral-institutional decline traced through to Chapter XV.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, was Frederick II doomed to political failure despite his personal brilliance?
questions.answer: Because the anti-papal forces of his time were genuinely pious and quasi-democratic, whereas Frederick's own aim was something like a restoration of the pagan Roman Empire; his position as Emperor therefore compelled him to oppose the free cities and other politically liberal forces that might otherwise have allied with him against the Pope, even though in culture he was more enlightened than any contemporary ruler.
questions.explanation: Russell frames this as one of history's most interesting failures precisely because of this mismatch between Frederick's personal enlightenment and his structurally reactionary political position.

questions.prompt: What were the core beliefs of the Cathari (Albigenses), and how reliable is our knowledge of them according to Russell?
questions.answer: The Cathari were dualists who considered the Old Testament God a wicked demiurge, believed matter was essentially evil, denied bodily resurrection for the virtuous, and practiced strict asceticism (including vegetarianism, except fish) among an elite class of 'the perfected,' while ordinary believers lived more normally. Russell cautions that their tenets 'cannot be known with certainty' since we depend entirely on the testimony of their persecutors, who tended to attribute to new sects the traits of earlier ones on the basis of loose resemblance.
questions.explanation: This is an important methodological caution Russell applies to medieval heresy generally.

questions.prompt: Compare the founding ideals and subsequent institutional history of the Franciscan and Dominican orders.
questions.answer: Saint Francis founded his order on an ideal of radical, literal poverty and itinerant preaching, personally disliking learning; but within a generation the order (under Brother Elias) abandoned poverty, staffed much of the Inquisition, and in 1323 condemned as heretical its own 'Spiritual' faithful who tried to keep Francis's original vow. Saint Dominic, by contrast, adopted poverty merely as a tactical means to combat heresy, and his order committed itself to learning from early on (despite Dominic's own personal indifference to it), producing Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas and thereby achieving the intellectual synthesis of Aristotle and Christian doctrine.
questions.explanation: Russell treats the Franciscan trajectory as deeply ironic relative to Francis's character, while the Dominican trajectory (learning as instrumental to orthodoxy) proceeds more straightforwardly from its founding purpose.

questions.prompt: What was the Inquisition, when was it founded, and what were its basic procedures according to this chapter?
questions.answer: Founded by Gregory IX in 1233 to take over the increasingly burdensome work of ferreting out heresy from bishops, staffed mainly by Dominicans and Franciscans; after 1254 the accused were denied counsel; those found guilty had their property confiscated (to the crown, in France) and were handed to secular authorities for execution, with those authorities themselves liable to Inquisitorial scrutiny if they failed to carry out the sentence.
questions.explanation: Russell notes it was, on its own terms, 'very successful,' completely stamping out the Albigensian heresy at the outset.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, did secular rulers generally fail to ally with heretical movements in the thirteenth century, unlike in the Reformation?
questions.answer: Russell states this was 'largely because no existing philosophy could reconcile heresy with the claims of kings to dominion' -- that is, the thirteenth century lacked the political-theological framework that later Protestant rulers would use to justify breaking with Rome while retaining royal authority.
questions.explanation: This foreshadows the eventual development of such frameworks (via figures like Marsiglio of Padua and William of Occam, covered in Chapter XIV) that would make later anti-papal alliances possible.

flashcards.front: Who were Frederick II's parents, and where did he spend his childhood?
flashcards.back: Son of Henry VI and Constance (heiress of the Norman kings of Sicily); he grew up in Palermo, Sicily.

flashcards.back: He negotiated its peaceful restoration with the Muslims while still under excommunication, which angered Gregory IX even more than his earlier refusal to crusade.

flashcards.back: A dualist heresy holding matter to be evil, strongest in southern France.

flashcards.front: Trace the lineage Russell gives for Cathari doctrine.
flashcards.back: Marcion and the Gnostics (ca. 150 AD) to the Paulicians (Armenian sect) to the Bogomiles of Bulgaria to the Cathari/Albigenses of Italy and southern France.

flashcards.back: Peter Waldo (ca. 1170); they eventually appointed their own ministers and dispensed with Catholic priests.

flashcards.back: A sudden impulse of pity led him to dismount and kiss a leper while riding by.

flashcards.back: Dominic adopted poverty only as a tactical means to combat heresy and committed the order early to scholarship, unlike Francis, who personally disliked learning.
